doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Church organ, left-hand bass and playing with a bassist
summary: He learned on a church organ and Hammond, disdains keyboard players who aren't real organists, and discusses left-hand bass and how a bassist changes his thinking.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Is that where you got your first organ experience? In the church?

Yes. Played a real church organ. Then we got a Hammond, but mother majored in music and church music you know. She was back there with Mrs. Madam Willa Dobbs and them sisters, it was Rebecca Steel and all of them heavyweights. And these average organ players, they don’t know what a [inaudible] is. They’re really not organ players. They’re not piano players either. They’re somebody with keyboard skills and they want to get the organ sound so they, you know, got a keyboard and learned how to play left hand bass. But they’re not no organ players.

Yeah, I was just going to ask about left hand bass because that’s a passion of mine. And I was watching you on a video that someone did in their home. And you were really wailing on the B3 and you were doing the left hand bass. And it’s a powerful feeling because you can really control the music. You’re the bass player and the soloist, and the chordal person.
No different from Johann Sebastian Bach. I keep trying to tell these idiots you’ve got to build on cumulative knowledge you know, and you can’t reinvent the wheel yourself.
Do you think differently or play different — well I’m going to say do you think differently when you have a bass player?

Well it’s just like being a pianist, you play different from when you play solo piano than when you play with the orchestra you know. You think differently. But you play the same, but you think different. They say you have more freedom with a bass player but you’re in a wider arena anyway, so thinking different is par for the course. It’s a negative sum game. You know?
